column2: When the activity of the mind is absorbed in the Supreme Self, Brahman, free of alternatives, no such alternative is seen; whatever else there is remains mere talk.
This alternative called "the universe" is like an unreal imagining in the one Reality; in what is unchanging, formless and without distinctions, how can there be difference?
In the one Reality, empty of seer, seeing and seen and the like, unchanging, formless and without distinctions, how can there be difference?
In the one Reality, utterly full like the ocean at the end of an age, unchanging, formless and without distinctions, how can there be difference?
In which the darkness, the cause of delusion, has dissolved like darkness in light — in the non-dual supreme truth, without distinctions, how can there be difference?
In the supreme truth, of one nature, how can talk of difference dwell? In deep sleep, which is mere happiness, by whom is difference seen?
By the knowledge of the supreme truth there is no universe in Brahman, the real Self, free of alternatives; in the three times a snake has not been seen in a rope, nor a drop of water in a mirage.
This duality is only Maya; in ultimate truth there is non-duality — so scripture says directly, and it is experienced in deep sleep.
The non-difference of what is superimposed from its substratum is seen by the wise in the rope-snake and the like; alternatives live by delusion.
This alternative is rooted in the mind; when the mind is absent, there is none. Therefore concentrate the mind on the Supreme Self, the inner reality.

The wise man in absorption realises in his heart Brahman, the full — something of constant awareness, of pure bliss, incomparable, exceeding all bounds, ever free, desireless, boundless like the sky, without parts and free of alternatives.

The wise man in absorption realises in his heart Brahman, the full — free of Nature and its modifications, a being beyond imagining, of one uniform taste, without equal, far from any means of knowledge, established by the words of the Vedas, ever well known as "I."

The wise man in absorption realises in his heart Brahman, the full — ageless, deathless, of the nature of the reality that has no non-being, like a calm ocean, without name, free of the modifications of qualities, eternal, tranquil, one.

With a collected mind, behold the Self of undivided glory in its own nature; with effort cut the bond that smells of worldly existence, and make your manhood fruitful. (Contemplate the Self, free of all adjuncts, being-consciousness-bliss, non-dual, abiding in the Self; you will not have to go on the road again.)
Like a person's shadow, which is seen in the form of a mere appearance, this body, experienced through the fruit of karma, the great soul casts aside like a corpse, and does not take it up again.

Having reached the Self, of the nature of ever-pure knowledge and bliss, cast far away this adjunct, of the nature of inert filth. And never again remember it: a thing that has been vomited, if made the object of memory, only disgusts.
Having burned this (world) with its root in the fire of the real Self, Brahman free of alternatives, the best of the wise then stands of himself as the eternal, pure Self of knowledge and bliss.
Let the body, strung on the thread of prarabdha, go or stay like a garland on a cow; the knower of truth, whose mental activity has merged in Brahman, the Self of bliss, does not look at it again.
Having known the Self as undivided bliss, as his own nature, what does the knower of truth desire, or for whose sake, that he should nourish the body?
This is the fruit for the perfected yogi liberated while living: the tasting of the ever-blissful essence in the Self, within and without.
The fruit of dispassion is knowledge; the fruit of knowledge is withdrawal (from the world); the fruit of withdrawal is peace from the experience of the bliss of the Self.
If the latter is absent, the earlier is fruitless. Cessation (of activity) is supreme contentment, incomparable bliss arising of itself.

Freedom from agitation at visible sufferings is the fruit of knowledge that is presented (here). How could a man, having by discrimination come to loathe the manifold actions he did in the time of delusion, do them afterward?

The fruit of knowledge is cessation from the unreal, and the fruit of ignorance is seen to be engagement in it, as with a mirage and the like; otherwise what visible fruit would there be for the knowers?
If the knot of ignorance in the heart is destroyed entirely, how can an object be the cause of engagement by itself for one who has no wish?

The limit of dispassion is the non-arising of habit-impressions toward the enjoyable; the highest limit of knowledge is the non-arising of the sense of "I"; and the limit of withdrawal is the non-arising (of any mental activity) for those whose activity is merged.

One whose mental activity always abides as Brahman, whose thought of external objects is gone, who takes in objects offered by others as a sleepy man or a child does, who sees this world like a world seen in a dream, and only occasionally regains awareness — such a person is rare on earth, blessed, revered: he enjoys the fruit of endless merit.
This ascetic of steady wisdom, who enjoys ever-lasting bliss, whose self is merged in Brahman alone, unchanging and actionless —

The activity of the mind that plunges into the oneness of the purified Brahman and Self, free of alternatives and of mere consciousness, is called wisdom (prajna). One in whom it is well established is said to be of steady wisdom.
He whose wisdom is steady, whose bliss is unbroken, and to whom the manifold world is almost forgotten, is held to be liberated while living.
Though his mind is merged, he is awake, free of the characteristics of waking; one whose knowledge is free of habit-impressions is held to be liberated while living.
One for whom the play of worldly existence has ceased, who, though having parts, is without parts, whose mind is free of anxiety — he is held to be liberated while living.
One who, though having a mind, is mindless; who, though this body persists, following him like a shadow, has no "I" and no "mine" — this is the mark of one liberated while living.
Non-pursuit of the past, no brooding on the future, and even indifference to what comes — these are the marks of one liberated while living.
Looking on all alike, in this world of things marked by merits and faults and different by nature, is the mark of one liberated while living.
Equal vision in the Self on the coming of desired and undesired objects, and unchangedness in both, is the mark of one liberated while living.
The ascetic's lack of awareness of within and without, because his mind is absorbed in tasting the bliss of Brahman, is the mark of one liberated while living.
One who, free of the feeling "mine" and "I" in body, senses and duties to be done, remains indifferent, has the mark of one liberated while living.
He is held to be liberated while living who has known, by the power of scripture, his state as Brahman, and is free from the bonds of worldly existence.
He is held to be liberated while living in whom the feeling "I" in body and senses and the feeling "this" in what is other never arise anywhere.

He is held to be liberated while living who is always free of the evil habit-impressions of the soul, the Lord and the world; he who by wisdom never sees a difference between the inner Self and Brahman, or between Brahman and creation, has the mark of one liberated while living.
He is held to be liberated while living who remains equal-minded when honoured by the good and tormented by the wicked.
He is liberated — the ascetic in whom objects sent by others, having entered, dissolve as being alone, like river-streams in the ocean, and produce no change.
For one who has known the truth of Brahman there is no worldly existence as before; if there is, he has not known his state as Brahman, but is still turned outward.
If it be said that he still wanders because of the force of old habit-impressions — no, because of the knowledge of oneness with the Real, habit-impression grows weak.
Even for the most lustful man, desire is checked toward his mother; so for the wise who has known Brahman, full bliss.
In one devoted to meditation, outward perceptions are seen; scripture says these are his prarabdha, from seeing the fruit.
As long as there is experience of pleasure and the like, so long prarabdha is held to exist; the arising of a fruit is preceded by action; without action, nowhere.
By the knowledge "I am Brahman," the accumulated (karma) gathered over hundreds of crores of ages dissolves, as the works of a dream on awakening.
Whatever merit or terrible sin was done in a dream — what does it lead to for one who has risen from sleep: heaven or hell?
Having known himself as unattached and indifferent like space, he is never touched by any karma that is to come.

The ascetic is not touched at all; the sky is not smeared by the smell of liquor through contact with a pot; so the Self is not touched by the properties of its adjuncts through association with them.
Prarabdha karma begun before the rise of knowledge is not destroyed by knowledge; it does not stop without giving its fruit, like an arrow shot at a target.
An arrow loosed with the notion "tiger" — afterward, once it is seen to be a cow — does not stop; it pierces the target with full speed.

Prarabdha is indeed stronger for the wise: it is exhausted by experience; accumulated and future works dissolve in the fire of right knowledge. For those who, seeing the oneness of Brahman and Self, are always established in identification with it, these three do not exist at all; they are Brahman itself, without qualities.
For a sage who abides in the Self as Brahman alone, free of identification with adjuncts, talk of the presence of prarabdha is not proper, like talk of dream-objects for one awake.
An awakened person does not make "I," "mine" and "this" in an appearing body, or in the world which serves the body; rather he stays awake in himself.
He has no desire to justify false things, and no collecting of that world is seen; if he engaged in a false object, he would not be free of sleep.
Likewise, one who abides in the Supreme Brahman remains as the real Self and sees nothing else; his memory of eating, releasing and the like is like memory of things seen in a dream.
The body is made by karma; let prarabdha be attributed to it. It is not proper for the beginningless Self; the Self is not made by karma.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting — so scripture, whose word never fails, says; for one who abides as that, where is the notion of prarabdha?
Prarabdha holds when one stands as the body; but identification with the body is not accepted (by the wise); therefore give up prarabdha.
The attribution of prarabdha even to the body is only delusion; how can the superimposed exist? How can the unreal be born? How can the unborn be destroyed? How can prarabdha exist for the unreal?
If by knowledge the effect of ignorance is destroyed with its root, "how does this body stand?" — this doubt troubles the dull.

Scripture speaks of prarabdha to satisfy such people from the external point of view, and not to teach the wise the truth of the body and the like; for the meaning of scripture has for its object the ultimate reality alone.
Full, without beginning or end, immeasurable, unchanging — Brahman, one alone, non-dual; there is no multiplicity here at all.
A mass of being, a mass of consciousness, eternal, a mass of bliss, actionless — Brahman, one alone, non-dual; there is no multiplicity here at all.
Inner, of one taste, full, infinite, facing all sides — Brahman, one alone, non-dual; there is no multiplicity here at all.
Not to be given up, not to be taken up, not to be imposed, without support — Brahman, one alone, non-dual; there is no multiplicity here at all.
Without qualities, without parts, subtle, free of alternatives, stainless — Brahman, one alone, non-dual; there is no multiplicity here at all.
Whose nature cannot be pointed out, beyond the reach of mind and speech — Brahman, one alone, non-dual; there is no multiplicity here at all.
Rich in being, self-established, pure, awake, incomparable — Brahman, one alone, non-dual; there is no multiplicity here at all.
Great ascetics, free from attachment, having given up enjoyments, tranquil, well self-controlled, having known this supreme truth, attain at the end the highest peace through union with the Self.
You too, having reflected on this supreme truth, the Self's own nature, a mass of bliss, and having shaken off the delusion imagined by your own mind, be liberated, fulfilled and awakened.
By absorption, with a well-steadied mind, behold the truth of the Self with the eye of clear knowledge; if what has been heard is examined without doubt and rightly, it is not questioned again.

In gaining the Self, whose nature is truth, knowledge and bliss, and in release from the bond of ignorance, scripture, reasoning and the teacher's words are authority, and the inwardly established experience of one's own Self is the (final) authority.
Bondage, liberation, contentment, worry, health, hunger and the like are known by oneself alone; the knowledge of others is only inference.
Teachers and scriptures instruct as bystanders; the wise man crosses only by wisdom, by the grace of the Lord.
Having himself known by his own experience his undivided Self, the perfected one should stand facing it, in the Self by the Self, free of alternatives.

This is the exposition of the conclusions of the Vedanta: Brahman alone is the individual, and the whole world; liberation is abiding in the undivided form; scripture is the authority for Brahman being without a second.

Having known the supreme Truth — "Brahman is non-dual" — by the words of the teacher, by the authority of scripture and by his own reasoning, with senses stilled and self collected, he became established in the Self, with an unmoving form.
Having concentrated the mind for some time on the Supreme Brahman, established in the Self, and having risen after a while from supreme bliss, he spoke these words.

On rising, my intellect is destroyed and activity has slipped away, through the realisation of the oneness of Brahman and the Self. I do not know this, nor do I know 'not this'; I know neither what nor how much happiness there is — it is boundless.

The majesty of the ocean of Supreme Brahman, filled with the flood of the nectar of the bliss of the Self, cannot be told by speech or thought. My mind, taking on the nature of a hailstone dissolved in the ocean, has merged in a tiny fraction of it and is now at rest, of the nature of bliss.
Where has this world gone? By whom was it taken? In what has it dissolved? It was seen by me just now — and it is not; is that not a great wonder?
What is to be given up, what to be taken? What is other, what is different, in the great ocean of Brahman, full of the nectar of undivided bliss?
I see nothing here, hear nothing, know nothing; I am distinct, by my own Self, of the form of ever-lasting bliss.
Homage, homage to you, teacher, great soul, free from attachment, the best of the good; embodiment of the taste of eternal, non-dual bliss, vast, ever the abode of boundless compassion.

By the falling of the thick moonlight of whose glance the weariness born of the heat of worldly existence has been shaken off, I have in a moment reached the imperishable state of the Self, the bliss of undivided majesty.
Blessed am I, my task is done; I am liberated from the seizure of worldly existence; I am of the nature of eternal bliss, I am full, by your grace.
I am unattached, I am bodiless, I am markless, I am imperishable; I am tranquil, I am infinite, I am stainless, I am ancient.
I am the unwearied; I am not the doer, not the enjoyer; I am unchanging, actionless; I am of the nature of pure knowledge; I am the alone, the ever-auspicious (Sadashiva).
